topic: @Transactional boundary that silently swallowed a refund
question: Riley Okonkwo has a Harbor Bike Co refund that returned 200 from refund-service — same Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.5 modular monolith as payment-service — but the ledger never moved and the payment is still COMPLETED. Someone caught an exception inside the @Transactional method and logged it. Explain the transaction boundary, why the refund was silently swallowed, and how you would fix it without a heroic double-write.
followUps: What happens if the same class calls this.refund() instead of going through the proxy?
Checked versus unchecked exceptions and rollback rules?
expectedConcepts: Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions that leave the proxy
Swallowed exceptions cause commit of a partial/no-op success
Self-invocation skips @Transactional
Ledger and refund row must share one boundary
engineerAnswer: If you catch the exception inside @Transactional and return normally, Spring commits. The API can look successful while the ledger write never happened. I would let the exception propagate.
seniorAnswer: RefundApplicationService should be the boundary, not the controller. PaymentPosting or ledger work must join that transaction. If a catch block logs and returns, Spring sees a clean method and commits whatever was flushed — or commits nothing useful and still returns 200. Self-invocation of a @Transactional helper does nothing. I fix by failing the request, marking rollback, and letting the client retry with the same idempotency key. I do not add a second 'compensate' write from the catch block.
staffAnswer: I want a test that throws after the refund row save and asserts no commit and no 200. I review rollbackFor if someone used a checked exception. I look for @Transactional on private methods and for REQUIRES_NEW that committed the refund row while the ledger failed. I will not 'fix' it by bouncing a task. I will not tell Priya this is a GC event. I add a metric for refund_commit_failed and a reconciliation query, but the code fix is the boundary.
principalAnswer: A 200 with a missing ledger line is a money defect. The standard is one transaction, exceptions leave the proxy, idempotent retry. I will not accept a catch-and-return as 'resilience.' I will not accept ND-in-Docker to get JTA as a substitute for a correct Spring boundary. Reconciliation is a backstop, not the design. Modular monolith stays valid: refund-service can share the ledger transaction in-process.
commonMistakes: Catching the exception, logging it, and returning 200 so the API 'stays up.'
Calling this.refund() on the same class and thinking @Transactional ran.
Adding REQUIRES_NEW on the refund row so something always commits.
scoreRubric: Engineer: swallowed exception commits. Senior: proxy boundary, self-invocation, fail and retry. Staff: tests for rollbackFor and REQUIRES_NEW. Principal: money-defect standard; JTA/ND-in-Docker is not the fix; monolith in-process TX is valid.

topic: Spring Security vs Jakarta security on Liberty
question: BayPay's production payment-service is Spring Boot 3.5.5 on Java 21 with Spring Security in front of POST /api/v1/payments. Morgan Hale still has a Liberty lab with Jakarta Security annotations on an older WAR. A senior candidate: compare the two models, what you would keep equivalent for Harbor Bike Co, and what you would refuse to run as production.
followUps: Where does authentication live versus method authorization on each stack?
Why is mixing both filters on one Boot app a failure class?
expectedConcepts: Spring Security filter chain vs Jakarta Security / SecurityContext
Same product rules: mTLS or JWT at the edge, method security on money writes
Do not double-wrap or disable security 'for the lab' in prod
Liberty leftover is not the Fargate estate
engineerAnswer: Spring Security uses a filter chain and annotations like @PreAuthorize. Jakarta Security on Liberty uses HttpAuthenticationMechanism and @RolesAllowed. Both should deny an unauthenticated create.
seniorAnswer: I would keep one security stack per process. On Boot, the ALB or API Gateway plus Spring Security must authenticate the caller before Bean Validation; method security guards refund and admin. On Liberty, Jakarta Security plus server constraints do the same job. I will not enable both Spring Security and a leftover Jakarta filter on the same payment-service — that is an order-of-filters defect. I will not copy Liberty role names from dmgr-east into Fargate and call it done.
staffAnswer: I want a threat model: merchant identity, service-to-service, and actuator. Spring Security resource-server JWT is the Boot default I would review; Jakarta Security is fine on a true Liberty runtime with an owner. I reject security:none profiles in any image Jordan ships. I reject mixing BASIC in the WAR and OAuth on the ALB without a written identity story. I keep PAN out of tokens and logs.
principalAnswer: Production identity is the Boot path on Fargate, not Morgan Hale's cell. I will not fund ND-in-Docker so we can 'keep Jakarta Security.' I will not accept two authoritative security filters. Equivalent product rules — who may create, who may refund — must be written once and mapped, not reinvented per runtime. Modular monolith may host both payment and refund if the method security is consistent.
commonMistakes: Running Spring Security and Jakarta Security filters in one app 'to be safe.'
Disabling security in a prod-like profile because the lab used permitAll.
Treating the leftover Liberty cell as the production identity provider.
scoreRubric: Engineer: names both models and an unauthenticated deny. Senior: one stack per process, method security on writes. Staff: threat model, no security:none, no PAN. Principal: Boot is prod estate; no ND-in-Docker; consistent rules across modules.

topic: OpenEntityManagerInView in a payment worker
question: Someone enabled OpenEntityManagerInView on BayPay's Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.5 payment-service and the same default leaked into the transaction-worker that posts Harbor Bike Co ledger lines. Staff-level: what OSIV is for, why it is the wrong default on a payment worker, and what lazy-load failures you would rather see.
followUps: How does OSIV extend the persistence context past the @Transactional method?
What happens to connection hold time and Hikari under Avery Chen load?
expectedConcepts: OSIV keeps the EntityManager open for the view/request
Workers have no view; OSIV holds connections across extra work
LazyInitializationException is a signal to fix the query
Explicit transaction + fetch plan on the posting path
engineerAnswer: OpenEntityManagerInView keeps the JPA session open after the service method so a view can lazy-load. A worker is not a view, so I would turn it off and fetch what I need in the transaction.
seniorAnswer: On a web request OSIV can hide LazyInitializationException by holding the persistence context until the JSON is written — and it holds a JDBC connection while Jackson walks Payment. On transaction-worker there is no view; OSIV still opens an EM around the listener and can hold Hikari connections across JMS handling or extra logging. I disable spring.jpa.open-in-view for the worker (and I prefer it off for the API too). I want a fetch join or a DTO query inside @Transactional so Avery's post does not lazy-load Account after commit.
staffAnswer: I treat OSIV-on as a review fail for any money worker. I measure Hikari active time with OSIV on versus off under Harbor Bike Co replay. I would rather see a lazy-load exception in CI than a connection leak in prod. I set open-in-view=false in shared config and only allow a documented exception on a read-only admin UI, never on posting. I will not raise the pool to hide OSIV hold time, and I will not raise -Xmx.
principalAnswer: Default is OSIV off on payment-service and workers. Lazy load in a worker is a design bug, not a reason to keep the session open. I will not accept OSIV as 'Jakarta compatibility.' I will not move posting to ND-in-Docker to get a different persistence context. The modular monolith may share repositories; each process still owns its persistence-context lifetime.
commonMistakes: Leaving open-in-view true because it is the Boot default.
Raising Hikari max when OSIV holds connections through JSON or JMS.
Catching LazyInitializationException and opening a new session per field.
scoreRubric: Engineer: OSIV is for views; workers should fetch in-TX. Senior: connection hold and fetch plans. Staff: review fail, measure pool hold, OSIV off. Principal: org default off; no ND-in-Docker; per-process persistence lifetime.

topic: JTA vs Spring transactions when a JMS send must enlist
question: Staff interview: payment-service on Spring Boot 3.5.5 / Java 21 writes the Harbor Bike Co ledger and must send a JMS PaymentAuthorized event so notification-service fires. If the JDBC commit succeeds and the send fails, Avery Chen's merchant is wrong. When do you enlist JMS in JTA, when do you keep Spring DataSourceTransactionManager plus an outbox, and what do you refuse?
followUps: What does last-resource optimization risk on a Boot JVM without a full JTA manager?
How does the modular monolith change whether you need XA today?
expectedConcepts: Spring @Transactional is usually local JDBC, not XA
JTA/XA enlists JDBC and JMS in one 2PC
Transactional outbox avoids XA for most Boot deployments
Liberty JTA vs Boot Atomikos / Narayana — do not invent ND-in-Docker
engineerAnswer: A local Spring transaction commits the database even if the JMS send fails. JTA would enlist both. An outbox table written in the same JDBC transaction is another way.
seniorAnswer: Today the modular monolith can publish in-process and skip the broker. If we extract notification, I will not pretend @Transactional on the service enlists JMS. I prefer an outbox row in the same JDBC transaction, then a poller sends JMS — at-least-once with idempotent consumers. I would only take JTA/XA if we already have a manager we operate (Liberty JTA, or a reviewed Narayana) and we have tested rollback of both legs. I will not add Atomikos on a Friday SEV.
staffAnswer: I draw the failure: DB commit / send fail, send success / DB rollback, and broker replay. XA solves the first two at the cost of heuristic mixed outcomes and a transaction manager to page. Outbox solves them with operational simplicity and a reconciliation query Priya can alert on. I reject last-resource gamble as a silent default. I reject running this on ND-in-Docker 'because WAS had JTA.' If we are on Liberty for real, I will use the server's JTA with an owner, not a second TM.
principalAnswer: Default for Boot on Fargate is local Spring transactions plus outbox, not XA. JTA is allowed on a supported Liberty runtime with a named owner — not as a reason to keep a leftover cell, and never as ND-in-Docker. Dual-write without a pattern is a money defect. Modular monolith in-process notification remains a valid way to avoid this distributed problem entirely.
commonMistakes: Assuming @Transactional enlists JMS on a local DataSourceTransactionManager.
Adding XA mid-incident without a transaction manager owner.
Recommending ND-in-Docker to 'get JTA for free.'
scoreRubric: Engineer: local TX vs JTA vs outbox. Senior: prefers outbox, XA only if operated. Staff: failure matrix, rejects last-resource and ND-in-Docker. Principal: Boot+outbox default; Liberty JTA only with owner; in-process monolith valid.

topic: when Spring Boot on Liberty is the wrong runtime
question: A principal-level design review: Jordan Voss wants to run the Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.5 payment-service fat JAR inside WebSphere Liberty — or even ND — because 'that is our Java standard.' When is Spring Boot on Liberty the wrong runtime for BayPay, what would you run instead, and which answers fail this interview?
followUps: What operational contract does a Boot fat JAR on Fargate already satisfy?
When is Liberty actually the right host for a Jakarta-shaped module?
expectedConcepts: Boot on Fargate/K8s is the production payment-service shape
Liberty is right for Jakarta EE apps that use server JTA/JCA — not a decorative host
Never ND-in-Docker
Two classloaders / two metrics stacks are a cost, not a free standard
engineerAnswer: If the app is a Spring Boot fat JAR with its own Tomcat and Actuator, putting it inside Liberty adds a second server you do not need. I would run the JAR on Fargate.
seniorAnswer: Spring Boot on Liberty is wrong when we only want a process supervisor: we pay for two servlet stacks, two health models, and a classloader story we do not use. Harbor Bike Co creates already work on port 8080 with Boot actuators. Liberty is right when the module is Jakarta EE and needs server JTA, JCA, or a WAR the platform team already operates — with an owner, not a leftover cell. I will not wrap the Boot JAR in ND to satisfy a standard.
staffAnswer: I compare failure domains: Fargate task replace versus Liberty rolling app update versus a cell. I count who pages on classloader leaks versus OOM 137. If the only reason is 'Java apps go on Liberty,' I write a dissent. I allow a documented Liberty host for a Jakarta adapter, with Sam owning the image and Priya owning the SLO. I refuse mixing Boot actuators and Liberty monitor in one SEV without a map.
principalAnswer: I will sign Boot on Fargate for payment-service. I will sign Liberty for a genuine Jakarta workload with JTA/JCA and a platform owner. I will not sign Spring Boot on Liberty as a decorative standard, and I will never sign ND-in-Docker. Modular monolith on a single Boot JVM is valid. Leftover dmgr-east is not spare capacity and not a runtime strategy.
commonMistakes: Recommending ND-in-Docker as the enterprise-standard host.
Putting a Boot fat JAR on Liberty with no Jakarta features used.
Using Morgan Hale's leftover cell as production capacity.
scoreRubric: Engineer: fat JAR does not need a second server. Senior: when Liberty is real vs decorative. Staff: failure-domain comparison and dissent. Principal: Boot/Fargate for payments; Liberty only for Jakarta-with-owner; never ND-in-Docker.

topic: Actuator exposure vs production attack surface
question: Jordan Voss enabled Spring Boot 3.5.5 Actuator on payment-service so Priya Nair can scrape health. A developer opened /actuator/env and /actuator/heapdump on the ALB hostname. In this Java 21 interview, what do you expose, what do you lock down, and how do liveness and readiness stay available for Harbor Bike Co traffic without handing out the process?
followUps: Which two health endpoints does the Fargate target group need?
Why is heapdump on a public path a SEV-class exposure?
expectedConcepts: Expose liveness and readiness only on the probe path
env, heapdump, logfile, beans are sensitive
Separate management port / network policy
No PAN or secrets in actuator output
engineerAnswer: I would expose /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness for probes. I would not expose env or heapdump on the public ALB.
seniorAnswer: Probes stay on 8080 or a management port that only the load balancer and kubelet can reach. I set management.endpoints.web.exposure.include to health — maybe prometheus on a scrape network — and I leave heapdump, env, configprops, threaddump off the internet. A heapdump endpoint is a production freeze and a PII path. Env can leak datasource URLs. Harbor Bike Co creates do not need those endpoints to succeed.
staffAnswer: I want a written exposure list, a network policy, and a test that the ALB hostname returns 404 or 401 for /actuator/env. I review that health groups do not include downstream payment rails in liveness — fail readiness, not liveness, when Hikari is exhausted. I reject Actuator plus Spring Security permitAll. I reject attaching a heapdump from Actuator to Slack. No PAN, no BAYPAY_DB_PASSWORD in env.
principalAnswer: Actuator is part of the production attack surface, not a convenience switch. I will sign health and authenticated metrics; I will not sign anonymous dump endpoints. I will not accept 'we needed it for the SEV' as a reason to leave heapdump on. I will not put Actuator on ND-in-Docker to copy WAS admin. Modular monolith means one careful exposure list, not five open admin UIs.
commonMistakes: Exposing * or heapdump/env on the public hostname.
Putting secrets or PAN into environment variables that /actuator/env would show.
Failing liveness when a dependency is down and looping restarts.
scoreRubric: Engineer: health only, no public dumps. Senior: include-list, management port, readiness vs liveness. Staff: network policy, tests, no secrets. Principal: attack surface standard; no dump-for-SEV; no ND-in-Docker admin.

topic: Testcontainers strategy for payment persistence
question: Riley Okonkwo's payment-service tests on Java 21 / Spring Boot 3.5.5 use H2 for most slices and a Testcontainers Postgres for Harbor Bike Co create and replay. Design the strategy: what runs in H2, what must run in Postgres, and how you keep CI honest without making every test start a database.
followUps: Which idempotency or locking behaviors will H2 lie about?
How do you share one container across a test class without leaking rows between Avery cases?
expectedConcepts: H2 for unit/slice; Testcontainers for SQL fidelity
Unique constraints, isolation, JSON/UUID types
Reuse containers; truncate or transactional rollback between tests
No PAN in fixtures; DemoIds only
engineerAnswer: I use H2 for fast unit tests and Testcontainers Postgres for API tests that depend on real constraints, like idempotency unique keys for Avery's create.
seniorAnswer: H2 will not faithfully do Postgres unique violations, isolation, or some types. PaymentApiIT and replay tests should use Testcontainers. Domain tests for Money and the state machine stay in-memory. I reuse one Postgres container per class, wrap each test in a transaction or truncate tables, and I never put PAN in fixtures — DemoIds and amounts only. I fail the build if the container cannot start rather than silently falling back to H2 for those ITs.
staffAnswer: I split the suite so PR CI runs unit plus one Postgres IT module, and nightly runs the heavier concurrency create test. I pin the Postgres image version Jordan also uses in paper prod notes. I watch for tests that @DirtiesContext the whole Spring Boot 3.5.5 app per method. I reject a strategy that needs Docker-in-ND or a shared dev cell database. Flyway/Liquibase must run against the same container the IT uses.
principalAnswer: Persistence tests that guard money invariants run on real Postgres. That is a quality gate, not optional local flavor. I will not accept H2-only as the merge bar for idempotency. I will not accept ND-in-Docker as the Testcontainers host. The modular monolith can share one test database schema across modules; we do not need a database per extracted service to test uniqueness.
commonMistakes: Running idempotency uniqueness only on H2 and calling it done.
Starting a new container per test method and blowing CI time.
Loading PAN or live passwords into test fixtures.
scoreRubric: Engineer: H2 vs Testcontainers split. Senior: constraint fidelity, reuse, no PAN. Staff: CI layers, pinned image, migrations. Principal: Postgres as merge bar for money tests; no ND-in-Docker; shared schema valid.

topic: Jakarta EE mapping for a Spring-trained team
question: Staff coaching: BayPay's payment-service team is Spring Boot 3.5.5 / Java 21 fluent and must read a Jakarta EE Liberty module Morgan Hale left behind. Map Spring ideas to Jakarta for them — injection, transactions, validation, persistence — and tell me what you would not tell them to rewrite first.
followUps: What is the Jakarta pair for @Service plus constructor injection?
Where does @Transactional map, and where does UserTransaction appear?
expectedConcepts: @Service/@Component → @ApplicationScoped or @Stateless
Constructor @Autowired → @Inject
Spring @Transactional → Jakarta @Transactional / JTA
Bean Validation and JPA names already shared; do not rewrite the domain first
engineerAnswer: Spring @Service with a constructor becomes a CDI bean with @Inject. @Transactional has a Jakarta name too. @Valid and JPA look familiar. I would not start by rewriting Money.
seniorAnswer: I map PaymentApplicationService to an @ApplicationScoped or @Stateless bean with constructor @Inject of repositories. Spring's @Transactional maps to Jakarta transaction interceptor or container JTA — same 'exceptions must leave the boundary' rule. CreatePaymentRequest validation is already Jakarta Bean Validation. JPA entities in shared stay. I teach the team the server's DataSource and JTA, not a new domain model. I do not tell them to extract microservices to avoid learning CDI.
staffAnswer: I run a pairing map: IoC, TX, validation, persistence, security, messaging. I call out the traps: Spring proxies versus CDI interceptors, self-invocation still skips TX, OSIV is not a Jakarta default, and Liberty classloaders are a different leak class. I keep production payment-service on Boot; the Liberty module is a port, not a surprise rewrite. I schedule time for JNDI and JTA labs, not for ND-in-Docker. I use Avery Chen create as the same acceptance test on both stacks.
principalAnswer: I will fund a mapping guide and a shared domain, not a rewrite of Harbor Bike Co into two languages of money. Spring-trained engineers should become bilingual; they should not be told the modular monolith is invalid or that ND-in-Docker is how you learn Jakarta. Boot remains the production runtime unless a Jakarta-only adapter is evidenced. Same status codes, same idempotency, same no-PAN rule.
commonMistakes: Telling the team to rewrite the domain before they can map injection and TX.
Equating Spring @Transactional with a local TX while the Liberty module is JTA without saying so.
Recommending ND-in-Docker as the Jakarta training environment.
scoreRubric: Engineer: basic annotation map, do not rewrite Money. Senior: CDI vs Spring, TX boundary, shared JPA. Staff: trap list, pairing plan, same acceptance test. Principal: bilingual team, monolith valid, Boot stays prod, never ND-in-Docker.
